analysis.one_liner: Requires the government to negotiate Medicare drug prices, with competitive licensing for companies that refuse.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past committee referral to a subcommittee, so Medicare still cannot negotiate drug prices under the law passed in that Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the government to negotiate the prices Medicare pays for prescription drugs, ending a rule that currently forbids this. If a drugmaker refused to negotiate, the government could license other companies to make the drug while compensating the original maker. The negotiated prices would also cap what private insurers, federal programs, and pharmacies can charge uninsured people, and price spikes beyond inflation would face a steep tax. The bill was referred to five House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and their families, through lower premiums and drug costs; the roughly 30 million uninsured Americans, who would be charged no more than the negotiated Medicare price; and taxpayers, since federal programs and employer plans alike would be capped at negotiated prices.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the government to negotiate Medicare prices for expensive drugs, with the price capped at about the median price charged in comparable wealthy countries — far below typical U.S. prices.

If a drugmaker refuses to negotiate, the government can license other companies to make the drug and pay the original maker 'reasonable compensation' — a way to keep the drug available rather than letting a refusal stall negotiations.
Caps what pharmacies can charge uninsured people at the Medicare-negotiated price, subject to penalties.
Taxes 50–100% of the revenue from price increases above inflation, and levies a 100% excise tax on sales above the negotiated price, so companies cannot simply ignore the system.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, through lower Medicare and market-wide prices, a tax on price spikes exceeding inflation, and the risk of having their patents and data licensed to competitors if they refuse to negotiate.

drawbacks.text: The negotiated price must at minimum cover a manufacturer's research and development costs, and competitive-license compensation must also let the original maker recoup R&D costs — so the bill pays companies for their development spending even as it forces prices down, which supporters would call a fair compromise and critics a limit on savings.

Setting a negotiated price as a ceiling across private insurance and pharmacies involves the federal government in setting prices throughout the drug market, a significant expansion of federal power that the pharmaceutical industry and some economists argue could reduce returns on drug development and slow the pipeline of new medicines.

Because the bill never received a committee vote, none of its practical details — how quickly the Secretary could actually negotiate, or how courts would treat overriding patents and exclusivities — were ever tested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and concrete: lower prices for the most expensive drugs across Medicare, private insurance, federal programs, and for the uninsured, with a backstop (competitive licensing) that keeps drugs available even if companies refuse to deal. The main cost, if negotiated prices run low, could be less revenue available for drug development over time; the bill's own R&D-recoupment floor and license compensation try to limit that. Another honest drawback is administrative: wide-scale government negotiation and licensing is a heavy new regulatory apparatus, and the bill gives the Secretary broad discretion. On balance, the design is unusually aggressive but targets the steepest prices and preserves compensation for innovators.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to five House committees, landed in the Energy and Commerce subcommittee on health, and stayed there — no markup, no floor vote, ever.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 29, 2021 by Rep. Lloyd Doggett with 79 Democratic cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee plus four other committees (Ways and Means, Oversight, Veterans' Affairs, and Armed Services).
In August and September 2021 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed; the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 with no committee vote and no House floor vote.

A narrower version of the idea — Medicare negotiation without competitive licensing — did later become law in a different bill in the 117th Congress, but H.R. 4811's stronger provisions never received a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept the legal ban on Medicare price negotiation for another Congress, along with their exclusive pricing power; patients kept paying U.S. prices.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 79 cosponsors.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and the pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Fiercely opposed government negotiation and competitive licensing of patented drugs, lobbying against bills of this kind throughout the 117th Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a subcommittee or committee vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 80 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the House leadership never advanced the bill out of committee.

industries.note: The bill would end the legal ban on Medicare negotiation, cap U.S. prices near international levels, let the government license their patents if they refuse, and tax price spikes and above-negotiated-price sales. Their U.S. revenue and pricing power would shrink substantially.

Private and employer plans must honor Medicare-negotiated prices, cutting their drug costs — but their role as payers is unchanged, and some of the savings would flow to premiums and profits rather than patients.
Competitive licensing would create new opportunities for companies willing to manufacture licensed drugs, with preference for U.S. manufacturers, while they face FDA fast-track obligations.
